\chapter{Taking, Asking, Helping, Liking}
\label{ch:bn-conjunct-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can take, ask, help and say what I like and whom I love in Bengali, build a fresh verb out of any noun by putting \bn{করা} behind it, and say why liking happens to me while loving is something I do.}

Say āmār bhālo lāge and hear that you are not its subject, set it against āmi bhālobāsi where you are, place both beside the \bn{আমার} … \bn{আছে} shape that says 'I have', and run the chapter's four verbs back — neowā, jijñāsā kôrā, sāhājjo kôrā, bhālo lāgā. Six of the chapter's nine atoms. Two of the other three — the \bn{নেওয়া} compound and the noun-plus-\bn{করা} pattern — are retrieved by the very next lesson after the one that taught them; the third, the doubled \bn{য্য} of \bn{সাহায্য}, is taught in the penultimate lesson and genuinely is not revisited, which is recorded here rather than papered over with a claim the payoff does not make.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[neowā]{\bn{নেওয়া} (neowā) — \textquotedblleft{}to take,\textquotedblright{} and the verb that finishes other verbs}

\label{lesson:BN-C09-neowa}



\begin{quote}
Bengali rarely leaves a verb standing alone. This is the verb it props most of them up with — and the tail it wears will look familiar.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{নেওয়া}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{নেওয়া}} — \emph{neowā} — \textbf{to take}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{নিই} (\emph{āmi nii}), \textquotedblleft{}I take.\textquotedblright{} \bn{আপনি} \bn{নেন} (\emph{āpni nen}), respectfully.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{নেওয়া}} is \textbf{\bn{নে}} (\emph{ne}) + \textbf{\bn{ওয়া}} (\emph{-owā}). \textbf{\bn{ন}} is a dental \emph{n}, tongue on the teeth. The \textbf{\bn{ওয়া}} tail is the one every dictionary-form verb of this kind wears — you have it already on \bn{হওয়া}, \bn{যাওয়া} and \bn{খাওয়া}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{নেওয়া}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{নী}} (\emph{√nī}), \textquotedblleft{}to lead, to carry away.\textquotedblright{} It is a well-attested Indo-Iranian root — Avestan \emph{nayeiti}, \textquotedblleft{}he leads\textquotedblright{}; Sanskrit \emph{netṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}a leader,\textquotedblright{} which is why a politician in Kolkata or Delhi is a \emph{netā}. Beyond that branch the trail thins, and \textbf{English kept nothing from it}. No cousin will be manufactured for you here; some roots stayed home.

The lesson worth more than a cousin is what Bengali \emph{does} with the verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb that ends a compound}]
Put a verb into its \textbf{-\bn{এ}} form (\emph{likhe}, \textquotedblleft{}having written\textquotedblright{}; \emph{niye}, \textquotedblleft{}having taken\textquotedblright{}) and hang a second verb behind it. The second verb stops meaning what it means and starts colouring the first:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{compound} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\bn{লিখে} \bn{নেওয়া} (\emph{likhe neowā}) & write it \textbf{down} — take the writing for yourself \\
\bn{নিয়ে} \bn{আসা} (\emph{niye āsā}) & \textbf{bring} — come, having taken \\
\bn{নিয়ে} \bn{যাওয়া} (\emph{niye jāwā}) & \textbf{take away} — go, having taken \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Bengali has no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}bring.\textquotedblright{} It has \textquotedblleft{}come having taken.\textquotedblright{} And \bn{নেওয়া} is a noun as readily as \bn{লেখা} was: \textbf{\bn{দেওয়া}-\bn{নেওয়া}} (\emph{deowā-neowā}), \textquotedblleft{}giving-and-taking,\textquotedblright{} is the everyday word for dealings between people.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}neowā\textquotedblright{} — take — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi nii\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same tail four times — \textquotedblleft{}hôwā, jāwā, khāwā, neowā\textquotedblright{}
  \item write it down — \textquotedblleft{}likhe neowā\textquotedblright{}
  \item bring, then take away — \textquotedblleft{}niye āsā … niye jāwā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Bengali say \textquotedblleft{}bring,\textquotedblright{} having no word for it? (\textbf{\bn{নিয়ে} \bn{আসা}} — \textquotedblleft{}come having taken\textquotedblright{}; and \textquotedblleft{}take away\textquotedblright{} is \bn{নিয়ে} \bn{যাওয়া}.) Does English share \bn{নেওয়া}'s root? (\textbf{No} — √nī stayed in Indo-Iranian, and that is the honest answer.) Name two more Bengali verbs that are also nouns. (\textbf{\bn{লেখা}} \textquotedblleft{}a piece of writing\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\bn{দেখা}} \textquotedblleft{}a seeing\textquotedblright{} — every \textbf{-\bn{া}} form does it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jijñāsā kôrā]{\bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করা} (jijñāsā kôrā) — \textquotedblleft{}to ask,\textquotedblright{} which is wanting to know}

\label{lesson:BN-C09-jijnasa-kora}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 7 warned you about a knot of letters, then spared you it. Here it is, inside a word you will use daily — and the word is Chapter 7's verb with an appetite.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করা}} — \emph{jijñāsā kôrā} — \textbf{to ask}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমি} \bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করি} (\emph{āmi jiggāshā kôri}), \textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{} — two words, one verb.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{জিজ্ঞাসা}} is \textbf{\bn{জি}} + \textbf{\bn{জ্ঞা}} + \textbf{\bn{সা}}. The middle piece \textbf{\bn{জ্ঞ}} is the knot of \textbf{\bn{জ}} and \textbf{\bn{ঞ}} Chapter 7 named on √jñā — and Bengali never says \emph{jñ}. It says \textbf{gg}, so the spelled \emph{jijñāsā} is spoken \textbf{jiggāshā}, with the \emph{s $\to$ sh} tilt at the end.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{জিজ্ঞাসা}} is Sanskrit's \textbf{desiderative} of \textbf{√\bn{জ্ঞা}} (\emph{√jñā}, \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{}) — the form meaning \emph{wanting} to do a thing. \emph{Jijñāsati} is \textquotedblleft{}he desires to know\textquotedblright{}; \emph{jijñāsā} is the desire itself. Bengali took the noun.

So asking is not a separate idea here. It is \textbf{\bn{জানা} with an appetite} — and the root behind both is the one Chapter 7 traced: PIE \emph{*ǵneh\textsubscript{3}-}, English \textbf{know}, Latin \emph{nōscere} (\textbf{notice}), Greek \emph{gnôsis} (\textbf{diagnosis}). The doubled \emph{ji-} is the desiderative's signature: a quiet echo of the root, meaning \emph{reaching for} it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: any noun plus \bn{করা} is a verb}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{noun + \bn{করা}} \\
\midrule
\bn{কাজ} (\emph{kāj}), work & \bn{কাজ} \bn{করা} — to work \\
\bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} (\emph{jijñāsā}), a wanting-to-know & \bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করা} — to ask \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Chapter 5 built \emph{kāj kôrā} this way. It is more than a compound: it is \textbf{the} way Bengali makes verbs. The stock of true verbs is small and closed, while nouns pour in from Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English — each becoming a verb the moment \bn{করা} stands behind it. Learn a noun, learn a verb.

Last lesson’s compound stacks on top: \textbf{\bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করে} \bn{নেওয়া}} (\emph{jijñāsā kôre neowā}) — \textquotedblleft{}just go ahead and ask.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item spelling, then sound — \textquotedblleft{}jijñāsā … jiggāshā\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}āmi jiggāshā kôri,\textquotedblright{} I ask, and the root it grew from, \textquotedblleft{}jānā\textquotedblright{}
  \item a fact, then a person — \textquotedblleft{}āmi jāni\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}āmi tāke chini\textquotedblright{}
  \item go ahead and ask — \textquotedblleft{}jijñāsā kôre neowā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Bengali say \textbf{\bn{জ্ঞ}}, and what is \bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} literally? (\textbf{gg}, never \emph{jñ}; and \textbf{a wanting-to-know}, the desiderative of \bn{জানা}'s root.) Someone asks whether you know their brother — which knowing verb answers? (\textbf{\bn{চেনা}} — a person is known by acquaintance; \bn{জানা} is for facts.) How do you make a verb from a noun you met this morning? (\textbf{Put \bn{করা} behind it.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāhājjo kôrā]{\bn{সাহায্য} \bn{করা} (sāhājjo kôrā) — \textquotedblleft{}to help,\textquotedblright{} which is going along with someone}

\label{lesson:BN-C09-sahajjo-kora}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 6 said Bengali's inherent vowel leans to \textbf{o}, then admitted it could not show you. This word can — and it is the word you will most want when stuck.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{সাহায্য} \bn{করা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{সাহায্য} \bn{করা}} — \emph{sāhājjo kôrā} — \textbf{to help}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমাকে} \bn{সাহায্য} \bn{করুন} (\emph{āmāke sāhājjo kôrun}), \textquotedblleft{}please help me\textquotedblright{}; \emph{āmāke} is \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{সাহায্য}} is \textbf{\bn{সা}} + \textbf{\bn{হা}} + \textbf{\bn{য্য}}. The last piece is \textbf{\bn{য}} stacked on itself — a conjunct, how Bengali writes a doubled consonant.

\begin{sounds}
Two rules land at the end, neither a quirk. Bengali reads a doubled \textbf{\bn{য}} as \textbf{jj}, not \emph{yy}. And nothing is written after it, so it takes the \textbf{inherent} vowel, which leans to \textbf{o}: \emph{sāhājj\textbf{o}}, never \emph{sāhājja}.

Chapter 6 could not show that inherent \textbf{o} in \emph{ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch}, since none of the five ends in a bare consonant. This one does. \textbf{\bn{সা}} takes the \emph{s $\to$ sh} tilt, so the whole is \emph{shāhājjo}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{সাহায্য}} is Sanskrit \emph{sāhāyya}, \textquotedblleft{}companionship,\textquotedblright{} on \textbf{\bn{সহায়}} (\emph{sahāya}), \textquotedblleft{}a companion\textquotedblright{} — which is \textbf{\bn{সহ}-} (\emph{saha-}), \textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{√\bn{ই}} (\emph{√i}), \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} A helper \textbf{goes along with you}.

Both halves have secure English cousins. \emph{Saha-} is PIE \emph{*sem-}, \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}: English \textbf{same}, Greek \emph{homós} (\textbf{homogeneous}), Latin \emph{similis} (\textbf{similar}). \emph{√i} is PIE \emph{*h\textsubscript{1}ey-}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}: Latin \emph{īre} gives \textbf{exit} and \textbf{transit}; Greek \emph{ión} gives \textbf{ion}. So \textquotedblleft{}help\textquotedblright{} is \emph{same-going}, and English holds the pieces without ever building the word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: asking for help is where the respect ladder bites}]
Another noun + \bn{করা}, like \bn{জিজ্ঞাসা} \bn{করা}. The respect sits where Chapter 7 put it — in \bn{করা}’s ending:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who you are asking} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}help\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
\bn{তুই} (\emph{tui}, intimate) & \bn{সাহায্য} \bn{কর} (\emph{kôr}) \\
\bn{তুমি} (\emph{tumi}, familiar) & \bn{সাহায্য} \bn{করো} (\emph{kôro}) \\
\bn{আপনি} (\emph{āpni}, respectful) & \bn{সাহায্য} \bn{করুন} (\emph{kôrun}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \emph{kôr} to a stranger and you were not rude by accident, but in grammar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item spelling, then sound — \textquotedblleft{}sāhāyya … shāhājjo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ladder — \textquotedblleft{}sāhājjo kôr … kôro … kôrun\textquotedblright{}
  \item please help me — \textquotedblleft{}āmāke sāhājjo kôrun\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two noun-verbs of this chapter — \textquotedblleft{}jijñāsā kôrā … sāhājjo kôrā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \bn{সাহায্য} end in \emph{-o} with nothing written there? (\textbf{The inherent vowel} — the thing the five numbers could not show.) Which form to a stranger? (\textbf{\bn{করুন}} — \emph{kôr} is for \bn{তুই}.) What is a \emph{sahāya}? (\textbf{One who goes with you}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhālo lāgā]{\bn{ভালো} \bn{লাগা} (bhālo lāgā) — \textquotedblleft{}to like,\textquotedblright{} which happens to you}

\label{lesson:BN-C09-bhalo-laga}



\begin{quote}
Every verb so far has let you be the one doing it. Here is one that does not.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{ভালো} \bn{লাগা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভালো} \bn{লাগা}} — \emph{bhālo lāgā} — \textbf{to like}
\end{quote}

\bn{আমার} \bn{ভালো} \bn{লাগে} (\emph{āmār bhālo lāge}), \textquotedblleft{}I like it.\textquotedblright{} Not \emph{āmi} — \textbf{āmār}, \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{ভালো}} is yours from Chapter 3. The new half is \textbf{\bn{লাগা}}: \textbf{\bn{লা}} + \textbf{\bn{গা}}, \textbf{\bn{গ}} being a hard \emph{g} as in \emph{go}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{লাগা}} is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{লগ্}} (\emph{√lag}), \textquotedblleft{}to attach, to stick\textquotedblright{}: \emph{āmār bhālo lāge} says, literally, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}good sticks to me.\textquotedblright{}}

\textbf{\bn{ভালোবাসা}} (\emph{bhālobāsā}), \textquotedblleft{}to love,\textquotedblright{} is \bn{ভালো} plus \textbf{\bn{বাসা}}, a verb no longer used alone. Its origin is genuinely disputed; the commonest proposal is Sanskrit \textbf{√\bn{বস্}} (\emph{√vas}), \textquotedblleft{}to dwell\textquotedblright{} — love as housed in goodness. If so it carries a startling cousin, since \emph{√vas} is PIE \emph{*h\textsubscript{2}wes-}, \textquotedblleft{}to stay,\textquotedblright{} which became Old English \emph{wesan} and so English \textbf{was}. That \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{} is real, and stays open.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: liking lands on you; loving you do}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{word for word} \\
\midrule
\bn{আমার} \bn{ভালো} \bn{লাগে} & to-me good sticks — \textbf{I like it} \\
\bn{আমার} \bn{চা} \bn{ভালো} \bn{লাগে} & to-me tea good sticks — \textbf{I like tea} \\
\bn{আমি} \bn{ভালোবাসি} & \textbf{I love} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That \emph{āmār …} shape is how Bengali says \textbf{I have} — \bn{আমার} … \bn{আছে}, with \bn{আছে} carrying the weight and no future of its own to give.

\textbf{\bn{ভালোবাসা}} breaks the pattern on purpose: \emph{āmi bhālobāsi} puts you in the subject's chair. It is a noun too — \textquotedblleft{}love\textquotedblright{} itself — as \bn{লেখা} was \textquotedblleft{}a piece of writing.\textquotedblright{} One form serves everybody. The harmony has nothing to bite on: \emph{bāsi} and \emph{bāse} keep their \textbf{ā}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār bhālo lāge\textquotedblright{} — hearing \textquotedblleft{}to me,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}
  \item I like tea — \textquotedblleft{}āmār chā bhālo lāge\textquotedblright{} — the tea Bengali eats, \textquotedblleft{}chā khāwā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one you do — \textquotedblleft{}āmi bhālobāsi\textquotedblright{} — one form, whoever is speaking
  \item the eight verbs of these two chapters — \textquotedblleft{}bhābā, bojhā, pôṛā, lekhā, neowā, jijñāsā kôrā, sāhājjo kôrā, bhālo lāgā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who is the subject of \emph{āmār bhālo lāge}, and what else is built that way? (\textbf{Not you} — the good is; \bn{আমার} … \bn{আছে}, \textquotedblleft{}I have,\textquotedblright{} and \bn{আছে} has no future of its own to give.) Does \emph{āmi bhālobāsi} behave the same, and would a woman say it differently? (\textbf{No}, and \textbf{no} — loving takes you as subject; Bengali has no grammatical gender.) Name two verbs that are also nouns. (\textbf{\bn{ভালোবাসা}} \textquotedblleft{}love,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\bn{লেখা}} \textquotedblleft{}writing.\textquotedblright{}) Why \emph{bāsi}, not \emph{bosi}? (\textbf{Nothing to raise} — this stem has \textbf{ā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
